title: Salt preparations
learningObjective: Know the general rules for predicting the solubility of ionic compounds in water: • common sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble • all nitrates are soluble • common chlorides are soluble, except those of silver and lead(II) • common sulfates are soluble, except for those of barium, calcium and lead(II) • common carbonates are insoluble, except for those of sodium, potassium and ammonium • common hydroxides are insoluble except for those of sodium, potassium and calcium (calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble).; Understand acids and bases in terms of proton transfer; Understand that an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor; Describe the reactions of hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid and nitric acid with metals, bases and metal carbonates (excluding the reactions between nitric acid and metals) to form salts; Know that metal oxides, metal hydroxides and ammonia can act as bases, and that alkalis are bases that are soluble in water; Describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt, starting from an insoluble reactant; Describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt, starting from an acid and alkali; Describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of an insoluble salt, starting from two soluble reactants; practical: prepare a sample of pure, dry hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals starting from copper(II) oxide; practical: prepare a sample of pure, dry lead(II) sulfate

sections.title: Acids, Bases and Salt Preparations
sections.markdown:
Acids do not just sit in bottles waiting to be classified — they react. Chapter
16 (u2:c16) gave you the map: how to tell an acid from an alkali, how the pH
scale bands them, and what neutralisation looks like ion by ion. This chapter
is about what acids actually **do**: how they attack metals, how they are
neutralised by bases and carbonates, and how those reactions are turned into a
laboratory skill — making salts, on purpose, pure and dry. When the hydrogen of
an acid is replaced by a metal (or by the ammonium ion), the compound that forms
is called a [[salt]] — and by the end of this chapter you will be able to make
several of them from scratch.

Four ideas organise everything that follows. First, **the reactions of acids**:
with metals above hydrogen, with metal oxides and hydroxides, and with
carbonates — each with its own summary equation and its own observations.
Second, **the solubility rules**: which ionic compounds dissolve in water and
which do not, because the method you choose for making a salt depends entirely
on whether your starting materials and your product are [[soluble]] or
[[insoluble]]. Third, **the three preparation methods**: crystallising a
soluble salt from an insoluble reactant, running a titration when both
reactants are solutions, and precipitating an insoluble salt out of two
solutions. Fourth, **the theory underneath it all**: acids and bases defined by
proton transfer — an idea that explains why ammonia, with no hydroxide ions of
its own, still neutralises an acid.

:::prior-knowledge
Four earlier chapters load this one. From Chapter 16 (u2:c16) you need acids as
sources of hydrogen ions, alkalis as sources of hydroxide ions, and the
neutralisation ionic equation H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). From Chapter 14
(u2:c14) you need the reactivity series, because whether a metal reacts with a
dilute acid — and how violently — is decided by its position in that series.
From Chapter 7 (u1:c07) you need ionic compounds existing as separated ions in
solution, which powers every ionic equation here. From Chapter 5 (u1:c05) you
need balanced equations with state symbols, plus water of crystallisation —
the CuSO₄·5H₂O you calculated there is made for real in this chapter.
:::

:::exam-hint
Seven of this chapter's ten objectives are examined in both papers — Paper 1C
and Paper 2C. Three are chemistry-only and appear in Paper 2C only: preparing a
soluble salt from an acid and alkali (2.40C), preparing an insoluble salt from
two soluble reactants (2.41C), and the lead(II) sulfate practical (2.43C). The
recurring question shapes are: state whether a named compound is soluble or
insoluble; write the equation for an acid with a metal, a base or a carbonate;
describe a salt preparation experiment step by step; and identify the proton
donor and proton acceptor in a reaction. Watch the command words: *state* wants
a fact, *describe* wants the method in order, *explain* wants the proton or
ion story.
:::

:::misconception
"'Salt' means the salt you put on your chips." Sodium chloride is one salt out
of an enormous family — magnesium sulfate, zinc chloride, potassium nitrate,
ammonium chloride and lead(II) sulfate are all salts too. In chemistry, a salt
is any compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or
by the ammonium ion. Some salts are [[soluble]], some are stubbornly
[[insoluble]], some hold water of crystallisation in their crystals — and the
table-salt on your chips is simply the one your body happens to need in
largest quantity.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.34–2.37 orientation items. Before moving on, say in
one sentence what a salt is in chemistry (not the chips definition), name the
three lab acids this chapter reacts with everything, and state which three
objectives of this chapter are Paper 2C only. If you can also say why
solubility decides the preparation method, the route map for the whole chapter
is fixed in your head.
:::

sections.title: Salts
sections.markdown:
Every acid contains hydrogen. When that hydrogen is replaced by a metal, the
compound formed is called a [[salt]]. Magnesium sulfate is a salt, and so is
zinc chloride, and so is potassium nitrate. Sodium chloride — common salt — is
a salt too, but you do not normally make it in the lab because it occurs
naturally in enormous deposits; it is the exception that proves the rule.

Each acid founds its own family of salts. Sulfuric acid can be thought of as
the parent acid of all the sulfates: the salts formed from sulfuric acid are
all called sulfates. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, nitric acid gives
nitrates, ethanoic acid gives ethanoates and phosphoric acid gives phosphates.

| Acid | Formula | Example of salt | Name of salts |
|---|---|---|---|
| hydrochloric acid | HCl | NaCl | chlorides |
| nitric acid | HNO₃ | KNO₃ | nitrates |
| sulfuric acid | H₂SO₄ | CuSO₄ | sulfates |
| ethanoic acid | CH₃COOH | CH₃COONa | ethanoates |
| phosphoric acid | H₃PO₄ | K₃PO₄ | phosphates |

It does not matter if the replacement of the hydrogen cannot be done directly.
You cannot make copper(II) sulfate from copper and dilute sulfuric acid,
because they simply do not react — copper sits below hydrogen in the reactivity
series, as the next section explains. There are, however, other ways of making
copper(II) sulfate from sulfuric acid, and this chapter teaches all of them:
copper(II) sulfate is still a salt, whichever route delivers it.

Salts are also formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced with the
ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. These are [[ammonium-salt]]s — for example NH₄Cl (ammonium
chloride) and (NH₄)₂SO₄ (ammonium sulfate). Ammonium salts matter far beyond
the lab bench: ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate are two of the world's
most important fertiliser salts, which is why the nitrogen from nitric acid and
sulfuric acid ends up in the soil.

:::key-point
Of the common acids in the lab, nitric acid has much more complex reactions
with metals. You will not be asked about nitric acid reacting with metals at
International GCSE — the acid + metal rule in this chapter applies to
hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid.
:::

:::exam-hint
The examiner expects you to move between an acid and its salt family without
hesitation: given H₂SO₄, say "sulfates" and quote CuSO₄; given "nitrates", say
"from nitric acid, HNO₃". Learn the table above as five matched pairs. A
favourite follow-up asks why copper(II) sulfate cannot be made by adding copper
to dilute sulfuric acid — the answer (no reaction, copper below hydrogen) earns
the mark, and "make it with copper(II) oxide instead" earns the respect.
:::

:::misconception
"'Salt' is a vague word, so any white powder counts." A salt is precisely
defined: the compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a
metal or by the ammonium ion. Copper(II) sulfate is a salt even though it is
blue, and ammonium chloride is a salt even though no metal atom appears
anywhere in it — the NH₄⁺ ion plays the role the metal ion plays in other
salts.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.37 salt-family items. Cover the table and reconstruct
it: name the salt family and one example salt for each of the five acids. Then
answer in one sentence each: why can you not make copper(II) sulfate from
copper and dilute sulfuric acid, and what ion replaces hydrogen in an ammonium
salt?
:::

sections.title: Reactions of Acids
sections.markdown:
Before the practical methods come the reactions they are built on. Simple
dilute acids react with metals depending on their positions in the
[[reactivity-series]], and the rules are worth stating exactly:

- Metals below hydrogen in the series do not react with dilute acids. Copper,
  silver and gold are safe in dilute acid — which is why copper pipes survive
  decades of water service.
- Metals above hydrogen in the series react to produce hydrogen gas.
- The higher the metal sits in the reactivity series, the more vigorous the
  reaction. You would never mix metals such as sodium or potassium with acids,
  because their reactions are too violent to be useful or safe.

For metals above hydrogen, the reaction has one summary equation:

**metal + acid → salt + hydrogen**

A mnemonic holds the whole rule together: **MASH** — **M**etal + **A**cid →
**S**alt + **H**ydrogen. Magnesium ribbon dropped into dilute sulfuric acid is
the classic demonstration, and the next section watches it happen observation
by observation.

:::exam-hint
Questions love the boundary cases. A metal below hydrogen (copper) + dilute
acid: no reaction — and "no reaction, because copper is below hydrogen in the
reactivity series" is the full-mark answer. Sodium or potassium + acid: reacts
so violently it is never done. A mid-series metal (magnesium, zinc, iron):
reacts steadily to give a [[salt]] and hydrogen. If asked to compare two
metals, the higher one in the series fizzes faster — rate of fizzing tracks
reactivity.
:::

:::misconception
"'Metal + acid' works for every metal." It works only for metals above hydrogen
in the reactivity series, and it is only *practical* for the moderately
reactive stretch from magnesium to iron — below that the reaction is too slow
to bother with, and far above it the reaction is explosively fast. Copper,
silver and gold give no hydrogen with dilute acids at all, however long you
wait.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.37 acid+metal items. Answer cold: state the summary
equation for a metal reacting with a dilute acid; name the gas that forms; and
sort copper, magnesium, potassium and zinc into "reacts vigorously", "reacts
steadily" and "no reaction" with dilute hydrochloric acid.
:::

sections.title: Reactions Involving Magnesium and Acids
sections.markdown:
Drop magnesium ribbon into dilute sulfuric acid and every observation arrives
at once: rapid fizzing, a colourless gas that pops with a lighted splint (the
test for hydrogen), a reaction mixture that becomes noticeably warm as heat is
produced, and the magnesium gradually disappearing to leave a colourless
solution of magnesium sulfate. The equation tells the same story:

Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

This is a displacement reaction. The more reactive magnesium has displaced the
less reactive hydrogen from the acid. Remember that ionic compounds are present
as separate ions in solution, so in the magnesium sulfate solution the
Mg²⁺(aq) and SO₄²⁻(aq) ions are separated from each other — which is exactly
what makes the ionic-equation view below possible.

Repeat the experiment with dilute hydrochloric acid and the reaction looks
exactly the same — same fizzing, same pop, same warmth. The only difference is
the salt formed: a solution of magnesium chloride this time.

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

Why do two different acids give identical reactions? Because both contain the
same reactive particle. Acids in solution form ions: dilute sulfuric acid
contains hydrogen ions and sulfate ions; dilute hydrochloric acid contains
hydrogen ions and chloride ions. Write the sulfuric acid reaction out in full
and the sulfate ion sits on both sides, untouched:

Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂(g)

The sulfate ion has not been changed by the reaction. It is a
[[spectator-ion]], and so it is left out of the [[ionic-equation]]:

Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)

Repeating this with hydrochloric acid shows the chloride ions are spectators
too — strike them out and the same ionic equation appears again. The reactions
look the same because they **are** the same: all solutions of acids contain
hydrogen ions, so magnesium reacts with any simple dilute acid in the same way.

Zinc tells the same tale more slowly. Sitting lower down the reactivity series
than magnesium, zinc reacts with both acids at a gentler pace:

Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

And once the spectators are struck out, zinc's ionic equation matches
magnesium's exactly — only the metal's symbol changes:

Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)

:::exam-hint
The observation marks come in fours: *fizzing* (hydrogen given off), *pops
with a lighted splint* (the gas test), *temperature rises* (exothermic), *metal
disappears leaving a colourless solution* (the salt). For ionic-equation
marks, the examiner wants the spectator struck out — writing the sulfate or
chloride into the final ionic equation loses the mark. And the explain-mark is
one sentence: acids react identically because all acid solutions contain
hydrogen ions.
:::

:::misconception
"Fizzing when a metal meets an acid means carbon dioxide is bubbling off."
Carbon dioxide comes from carbonates, not from metals. Metal + acid gives
**hydrogen**, identified by the lighted splint pop. The limewater test never
enters a metal–acid question — if the gas pops with a lighted splint, hydrogen
is the only candidate, and the salt that forms contains the metal, not any
carbon.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.37 acid+metal observation items. Write the full
equation for magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid including state symbols,
then strike out the spectator ions to reach the ionic equation. Which two
observations prove the gas is hydrogen, and why do magnesium's reactions with
sulfuric acid and hydrochloric acid look identical?
:::

sections.title: Bases
sections.markdown:
Bases are substances that neutralise acids by combining with the hydrogen ions
in them to produce water. When referring to a [[base]] at this level, you
usually mean a [[metal-oxide]], a metal hydroxide or ammonia — that trio is
exactly what the specification names, and keeping it in your head is an exam
point in itself.

Metal oxides, such as copper(II) oxide and magnesium oxide, are bases. Heat
black copper(II) oxide powder with hot dilute sulfuric acid and the black solid
reacts to produce a blue solution of copper(II) sulfate:

CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)

All the metal oxide and acid combinations you will meet at International GCSE
behave in the same way as copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid: they
produce a [[salt]] and water. Most need to be heated for the reaction to
start — the cold beaker of acid and black powder does nothing until the
Bunsen flame arrives.

Copper(II) oxide is an ionic compound containing the O²⁻ ion, and that ion
explains the reaction: the H⁺ ions from the acid have combined with the O²⁻
ions to form water, H₂O. This is a [[neutralisation]] — the base has consumed
the acid's hydrogen ions. The general equation for the reaction of a metal
oxide with an acid is:

**metal oxide + acid → salt + water**

:::exam-hint
Two facts about bases earn marks again and again. First, the list: metal
oxides, metal hydroxides and ammonia can all act as bases (2.38 names exactly
that list — carbonates are *not* on it, even though they neutralise acids).
Second, the products: base + acid always gives a salt and water, never
hydrogen and never carbon dioxide — those belong to metals and carbonates
respectively. Most oxide–acid reactions need heating to start; carbonate–acid
reactions do not.
:::

:::misconception
"'Base' and 'alkali' are two spellings of the same word." They are not. A base
neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that is *soluble in water*. Copper(II)
oxide is a base but not an alkali — it will not dissolve, so it never gives an
alkaline solution. Sodium hydroxide is both. The next section turns this
distinction into equations you can write.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.37/2.38 base-reaction items. Write the equation for
copper(II) oxide with dilute sulfuric acid including state symbols, state the
general word equation for a metal oxide with an acid, and name the three
substance types that can act as bases in this specification.
:::

sections.title: Bases and Alkalis
sections.markdown:
An [[alkali]] is a base that dissolves in water — and the soluble metal oxides
show how one becomes the other. Some metal oxides are soluble in water and
react with it to form solutions of metal hydroxides:

Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)

All the Group 1 oxides do this reaction, so for potassium oxide:

K₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2KOH(aq)

Most other metal oxides are not soluble in water. Calcium oxide dissolves
slightly to form calcium hydroxide:

CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq)

Another alkali you will meet is [[ammonia-solution]] — a solution of ammonia.
The ammonia reacts with the water to form ammonium ions and hydroxide ions:

NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

All these solutions contain hydroxide ions — and alkalis are solutions that
are a source of hydroxide (OH⁻) ions, so every one of them is an alkali. The
reversible arrow on the ammonia equation is doing real work: only a fraction
of the dissolved ammonia reacts at any moment, which is why ammonia solution is
weakly alkaline while sodium hydroxide solution is strongly alkaline.

All metal hydroxides react with acids in a [[neutralisation]] reaction. Mixing
sodium hydroxide solution with dilute hydrochloric acid gives a colourless
solution, so not much seems to have happened — but repeat it with a thermometer
in the beaker and the temperature rises several degrees, showing that a
chemical change has occurred. Sodium chloride solution has been formed:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

The [[ionic-equation]] for this reaction is the one that covers every acid–
alkali neutralisation:

OH⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l)

All neutralisation reactions between an acid and an alkali share it: the
hydroxide ions from the alkali react with the H⁺ ions from the acid to form
water. Everything else in the equation is spectators.

**Carbonates and acids.** Carbonates react with cold dilute acids to produce
carbon dioxide gas, with a summary equation of their own:

**carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide + water**

Green copper(II) carbonate reacts with the common dilute acids to give a blue
or blue-green solution of copper(II) sulfate, copper(II) nitrate or copper(II)
chloride, with carbon dioxide gas given off — recognisable because it turns
limewater milky. All three equations have the same form:

CuCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

CuCO₃(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

CuCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CuCl₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

Sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acid follows the same pattern:

Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

Show the ions and the carbonate story deepens. By not including the spectator
ions (the sodium and the chloride), the ionic equation for carbonate + acid is:

CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

Because carbonate ions react by accepting hydrogen ions, carbonate ions can be
classified as [[base]]s in proton-transfer terms — a preview of the theory at
the end of this chapter. In the practical specification, though, only metal oxides,
metal hydroxides and ammonia count as bases; carbonates are their own
reagent class.

:::exam-hint
The examiner rewards matching reagent to product: metal + acid → salt +
hydrogen; base + acid → salt + water; carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide
+ water. State the observations too — carbonate reactions fizz in the *cold*,
while metal oxides usually need heating, and the gas that turns limewater milky
is carbon dioxide, never hydrogen. For the ionic equation, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
scores for every acid–alkali pair; the carbonate ionic equation CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ →
CO₂ + H₂O is the extension-level version.
:::

:::misconception
"Sodium oxide must be an acid because it contains oxygen, or at least
neutral." Group 1 oxides are strongly basic: they react with water to make
hydroxide ions, which is the alkaline signature. The oxygen in Na₂O ends up as
O²⁻ ions that grab H⁺ from water — oxide ions are proton acceptors, the most
basic behaviour there is. Solubility, not oxygen content, decides acid/base
behaviour here.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.37/2.38 alkali and carbonate items. Write the
equations for potassium oxide with water and for copper(II) carbonate with
dilute hydrochloric acid, both with state symbols. Then explain in one
sentence why ammonia solution is an alkali even though NH₃ contains no
hydroxide — and give the ionic equation that covers all acid–alkali
neutralisations.
:::

sections.title: Notes on the Solubility Table
sections.markdown:
The solubility rules in the next section compress a whole lab's worth of
experience into six lines, and two honest caveats make them easier to use.
First, to keep the rules simple, they include one or two compounds — aluminium
carbonate, for example — that do not actually exist. Do not worry about these:
the problem will not arise at International GCSE. If a question names a
compound, treat the rules as if it exists and answer from the pattern.

Second, there is no sharp line between "[[insoluble]]" and "almost insoluble"
compounds. Nothing dissolves exactly zero. The substances picked out as almost
insoluble — calcium hydroxide is the famous example — include the more common
ones you will need elsewhere in the course, which is precisely why they get
their own special mention instead of being swept into the insoluble column.

The reason the exceptions cluster where they do is worth understanding rather
than memorising: the exceptions in the carbonates and hydroxides exist because
all sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble, so a sodium, potassium
or ammonium carbonate or hydroxide inherits that solubility and drags its whole
family towards the soluble side. Except for the carbonates and hydroxides,
most of these compounds are [[soluble]] — so the rules that actually need
learning are the exceptions in the sulfates and the chlorides. Learn those two
exception lists cold and the rest follows from the pattern.

:::exam-hint
Examiners set solubility questions straight from these rules: "state whether
silver chloride is soluble" (no — chloride exception), "is barium sulfate
soluble?" (no — sulfate exception), "is sodium carbonate soluble?" (yes — all
sodium compounds are). Note how the "almost insoluble" subtlety is itself
examinable through calcium hydroxide, whose slight solubility is what lets
limewater exist at all.
:::

:::misconception
"'Insoluble' means none of it dissolves — ever." Even the most stubborn
"insoluble" salts leave a trace of ions in solution; that trace is exactly what
acidified silver nitrate detects in the chloride test, and exactly what makes
calcium hydroxide solution (limewater) possible. Insoluble in practice means
"so slightly soluble that a solid is seen when you mix the solutions" — the
precipitate line you will meet later in this chapter.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.34 solubility-rule items. Say which two exception
lists need active memorising, and why the carbonate and hydroxide exceptions
exist at all. Then apply the rules: classify silver chloride, barium sulfate,
sodium carbonate and calcium hydroxide as soluble or insoluble.
:::

sections.title: Salt Preparations
sections.markdown:
The next sections teach the practical methods for making salts — and before any
apparatus is picked up, one decision has to be made, because the method you use
depends entirely on solubility. Which of the starting substances are [[soluble]]
in water, and is the salt you want [[soluble]] or [[insoluble]]? Answer that
and the method chooses itself; answer it wrongly and no amount of careful
technique will rescue the experiment.

The decision tree has exactly three branches, and every salt-preparation
question in the course is secretly asking you to walk it:

1. **Soluble salt from an insoluble reactant.** Add the insoluble solid
   (a metal, a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide or a carbonate) to acid in
   excess, filter off the leftover solid, crystallise the solution. This
   covers copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and the other workhorse
   preparations.
2. **Soluble salt from two soluble reactants.** When both reactants are
   solutions — as with all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts — there is no
   solid excess to filter, so an [[excess]] trick is impossible and a
   titration with an indicator does the measuring instead.
3. **Insoluble salt from two soluble reactants.** When the *product* is the
   insoluble one, no acid is needed at all: mix two solutions and the insoluble
   salt precipitates as a solid you can filter, wash and dry.

Each branch gets its own section, with the full practical detail the
examination statements demand.

:::exam-hint
"Describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of..." is a *describe*
question — the marks are for the method in order, not for chemistry theory.
The first sentence of your answer should signal the branch: "add excess
copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid" (branch 1), "titrate, then
repeat without indicator" (branch 2), "mix lead(II) nitrate solution with
sodium sulfate solution" (branch 3). Choosing the branch correctly is worth
more marks than any single step, because every later mark depends on it.
:::

:::misconception
"The method for making a salt depends on the acid you start from." It depends
on solubility — of the reactants and the product. Sulfuric acid appears in all
three branches: warming it with copper(II) oxide gives crystals (branch 1),
titrating it against sodium hydroxide gives sodium sulfate (branch 2), and
using it as the sulfate source for barium sulfate gives a precipitate (branch
3). Solubility decides; the acid follows.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.34/2.39 method-choice items. For each of these,
name the branch: making copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide; making
potassium nitrate from potassium hydroxide solution; making barium sulfate.
Then say what goes wrong in branch 2 if you try to use excess solid reactant
instead of a titration.
:::

sections.title: The Solubility Rules
sections.markdown:
Here are the rules for predicting the solubility of ionic compounds in water —
the specification's list, stated as you will use them:

- all sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are [[soluble]]
- all nitrates are soluble
- most common chlorides are soluble, except lead(II) chloride and silver
  chloride
- most common sulfates are soluble, except lead(II) sulfate, barium sulfate,
  silver sulfate and calcium sulfate
- most common carbonates are [[insoluble]], except sodium, potassium and
  ammonium carbonates
- most metal hydroxides are insoluble (or almost insoluble), except sodium,
  potassium and ammonium hydroxides; calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble in
  water

Two of these lines are the specification's own exceptions to know by heart:
common chlorides are soluble except those of silver and lead(II), and common
sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead(II). The fuller
sulfate list above adds silver sulfate, which is also extremely reluctant to
dissolve — worth knowing when the ion tests arrive in the next chapter, because
that reluctance is exactly what those tests exploit.

Notice the load-bearing first line: sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds
are always soluble, no matter what the rest of the rule says. That single line
rescues sodium carbonate from the insoluble-carbonate family, keeps potassium
hydroxide among the soluble hydroxides, and — as the next sections show — makes
the excess-solid method impossible for every sodium, potassium and ammonium
salt.

:::safety
Direct heating of the acid is not recommended in any of these preparations.
Wear eye protection and never evaporate a salt solution to dryness over a
direct flame. The acid is best heated in a boiling tube placed in a water
bath. Avoid skin contact with the crystals — several prepared salts, including
copper(II) sulfate, are harmful and irritating to both skin and eyes.
:::

:::exam-hint
Solubility marks are the cheapest marks in the paper — provided you quote the
exceptions exactly. The three insoluble chlorides-and-sulfates stars are
**silver**, **lead(II)** and **barium**; calcium joins the sulfate exceptions,
and calcium hydroxide is the special case that is only *slightly* soluble. A
full-credit answer to "is lead(II) chloride soluble?" is "no — common chlorides
are soluble except those of silver and lead(II)".
:::

:::misconception
"Calcium hydroxide must be insoluble, because most hydroxides are." Calcium
hydroxide is the deliberate exception-within-the-exception: slightly soluble.
That slight solubility is not a footnote — it is why limewater exists, why it
can turn milky in the carbon dioxide test, and why the solubility rules flag it
separately instead of filing it with the truly insoluble hydroxides.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.34 solubility items. Classify each as soluble or

:::

sections.title: Making Soluble Salts (except Sodium, Potassium and Ammonium Salts)
sections.markdown:
Making a [[soluble]] salt whose parent solid is insoluble always involves reacting a solid with an acid. You can use any of the following mixtures:

- acid + metal (but only for the moderately reactive metals from magnesium to
  iron in the reactivity series)
- acid + metal oxide or hydroxide
- acid + carbonate

Whatever mixture you choose, the method is basically the same: react the solid
with acid, remove the leftover solid, then crystallise the salt from the
solution. The classic worked preparation is copper(II) sulfate crystals from
copper(II) oxide — the specification's own practical (2.42).

**The practical, step by step.**

1. Measure 50 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker and heat it on a
   tripod and gauze using a Bunsen burner.
2. Add a spatula-full of black copper(II) oxide and continue heating. If all
   the copper(II) oxide disappears, add more until some is left in the beaker,
   stirring well to make sure no more will react. You have now added the solid
   in [[excess]] — more than enough to react with all the acid present. When
   copper(II) oxide is still left over, you know all the acid has been
   neutralised.
3. Filter off the excess copper(II) oxide and transfer the filtrate — the blue
   solution, which is copper(II) sulfate — to an evaporating basin. The
   formation equation is:

   CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)

4. Heat the solution to boil off some of the water and concentrate it. Keep
   heating until a saturated solution forms: dip a glass rod into the solution,
   and if crystals form on the rod when you remove it, the solution is close
   to saturation and crystals will soon form in it too.
5. Stop heating and allow the solution to cool slowly at room temperature so
   that larger crystals can form.
6. Remove the blue crystals by [[filtration]], or simply pour off the
   remaining solution.
7. Dry the crystals by blotting them with a paper towel, or leave them to dry
   in a warm place.

The same seven beats work for magnesium sulfate (acid + magnesium), for zinc
chloride (acid + zinc) and for any other soluble salt whose reactant leaves a
visible unreacted excess. Excess solid is the whole trick: the visible leftover
is the indicator that the acid is gone, and the filtration step then removes it
along with any insoluble impurities.

:::key-point
"'Anhydrous' means 'without water'." The word will matter in the next section —
evaporate a copper(II) sulfate solution all the way to dryness and you get the
anhydrous white powder, not the blue crystals the practical is asking for.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection throughout. Heating must be very gentle when concentrating
the solution — boiling salt solutions spit hot droplets of liquid and solid.
The water-bath rule from the solubility section applies here too: gentle,
indirect heat, never evaporate to dryness over a direct flame.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt,
starting from an insoluble reactant" (2.39) is scored in beats: warm the acid;
add the insoluble reactant in excess (say *why* — to ensure all the acid
reacts); filter to remove the excess solid; heat the filtrate to concentrate;
test for saturation with a glass rod; cool slowly to crystallise; filter the
crystals; dry them on paper towel or in a warm place. Miss the word *excess*
or forget to say why, and the neutrality of your product is unproven — that is
where the marks sit.
:::

:::misconception
"Add exactly the right amount of copper(II) oxide, then no filtering is
needed." Exactly-right amounts cannot be judged by eye, and unreacted acid
ruins the preparation. Adding excess solid and filtering it off is not a
safety-net habit — it is the proof that every drop of acid reacted, which is
what makes the final crystals pure copper(II) sulfate rather than a mixture
with acid hiding among the water.
:::

Question-bank join: spec 2.39/2.42 preparation-method items. List the seven
steps of the copper(II) sulfate preparation in order, naming the apparatus at
each step. Why is the copper(II) oxide added in excess, and how do you test
that the solution has become saturated before cooling?
:::

sections.title: Why Not Simply Evaporate the Solution to Dryness?
sections.markdown:
It would seem much easier to just boil off all the water rather than
crystallising the solution slowly — but evaporating a copper(II) sulfate
solution to dryness would not give you blue copper(II) sulfate crystals at all.
Instead, you would produce a white powder of [[anhydrous]] copper(II) sulfate.
The blue crystals and the white powder are the same compound with the same
formula unit — what differs is the water that the crystals carry inside their
structure.

When many salts form their crystals, water from the solution becomes
chemically bound up with the salt. This is called [[water-of-crystallisation]].
A salt which contains water of crystallisation is said to be [[hydrated]]. The
crystallisation half of the copper(II) sulfate preparation is therefore a
chemical change of its own, with its own equation:

CuSO₄(aq) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)

Five water molecules lock into the lattice for every copper sulfate formula
unit — the blue colour of the crystals belongs to that combined water. Boil
past this point and the water of crystallisation is driven off, the lattice
collapses into the anhydrous form, and the blue gives way to white. Slow
cooling is what lets the crystals take their water up in an orderly way; the
glass-rod saturation test from the last section tells you when to stop heating
and start cooling.

You have met this arithmetic before: Chapter 5 (u1:c05) worked the molar mass
of CuSO₄·5H₂O and the water-of-crystallisation calculations that go with it.
This chapter is where that dot-and-five-H₂O notation is actually made on the
bench — the practical in the last section exists precisely to deliver the
hydrated crystals, and stopping at the right moment is what separates a tray of
blue crystals from a spoonful of white powder.

:::exam-hint
Two equations, two products, one error to avoid. Crystallisation:
CuSO₄(aq) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) — blue hydrated crystals. Over-heating:
the water of crystallisation is lost and the white anhydrous solid remains.
Questions award the marks for naming water of crystallisation, writing the
dot formula correctly, and stating that evaporating to dryness gives the
anhydrous salt instead. The dryness rule — never evaporate to dryness — is now
chemistry, not just safety: it protects the very water the crystals need.
:::

:::misconception
"The blue crystals are copper(II) sulfate, and the white powder is some
different sulfate made by a side reaction." There is no side reaction and no
different compound — both are copper(II) sulfate. The crystals are the
*hydrated* form, CuSO₄·5H₂O, with five waters of crystallisation built into
each lattice; the powder is the *anhydrous* form with none. The colour change
from blue to white is the water leaving, which is why anhydrous copper(II)
sulfate turns blue again the moment water touches it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.42 crystallisation items. Write the crystallisation
equation for copper(II) sulfate, define water of crystallisation in one
sentence, and explain why evaporating the solution to dryness spoils the
preparation — name both products in your answer.
:::

sections.title: Making Magnesium Sulfate Crystals
sections.markdown:
The magnesium sulfate preparation runs the same seven beats as the copper(II)
sulfate practical, with one welcome difference: no heating is needed at the
reacting stage. Add [[excess]] magnesium to dilute sulfuric acid — the acid
does not have to be warmed, because magnesium sits high enough in the
reactivity series to react in the cold. As you add the magnesium, the reaction
mixture fizzes (hydrogen is given off). Keep adding magnesium until the fizzing
stops and some magnesium is left in the beaker — that leftover tells you all
the acid has reacted. The equation for the formation of the solution is:

Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

Again the solution is concentrated by heating it gently and then allowed to
crystallise. The crystallisation reaction is:

MgSO₄(aq) + 7H₂O(l) → MgSO₄·7H₂O(s)

Seven waters of crystallisation this time, not five — each hydrated salt
carries its own fixed number, which is why the crystallisation equations are
never interchangeable between salts.

**How do you know whether you need to heat the mixture?** Carbonates react with
dilute acids in the cold, and so does magnesium. Most other things you are
likely to use — copper(II) oxide chief among them — need to be heated for the
reaction to start. The rule of thumb: high-reactivity metals and carbonates
react cold; metal oxides and the slower metals need the warm acid.

:::key-point
[[methyl-orange]] is red in acidic solutions and yellow in alkaline ones. When
it is used as an indicator in titrations involving adding acid to alkali, an
orange colour is usually obtained at the [[endpoint]] — orange is a mixture of
the red and yellow forms. This detail matters two sections from now, when
methyl orange announces the endpoint of the sodium sulfate titration.
:::

:::exam-hint
Comparing the two crystal preparations is a reliable exam question. Magnesium
sulfate: excess magnesium, no heating to react, fizzing tells you the acid is
still there, stop when fizzing stops with metal left over. Copper(II) sulfate:
excess copper(II) oxide, warm the acid, no fizzing to watch — the leftover
black solid is your signal. The marks live in the *why*: excess guarantees all
the acid reacts, and the visible leftover proves it. Both crystallisations end
the same way: concentrate, glass-rod test, cool slowly, filter, dry.
:::

:::misconception
"Magnesium sulfate and copper(II) sulfate crystals must have the same formula
shape, so it is MgSO₄·5H₂O as well." The number of waters of crystallisation
is fixed for each salt and measured for each salt: magnesium sulfate heptahydrate
is MgSO₄·7H₂O, copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate is CuSO₄·5H₂O. Copying the
5 across is exactly the kind of slip that loses the equation mark — each
crystallisation equation states its own water count.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.39 preparation-variation items. Write the formation
equation and the crystallisation equation for magnesium sulfate. Which two
reagent classes react with cold dilute acid without heating, and what visible
sign replaces the leftover-black-solid signal in the magnesium case?
:::

sections.title: Making Sodium, Potassium and Ammonium Salts
sections.markdown:
The excess-solid method fails completely for sodium, potassium and ammonium
salts, and the reason is the first line of the solubility rules: all sodium,
potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble. The solid you add to the acid
would not only react with it — any excess would simply dissolve in the water
present. You would have no visible excess to filter off, and no simple way of
seeing when you have added just enough solid to neutralise the acid.

You normally make these salts from sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide
solution, or from ammonia solution — the carbonates work too. Fortunately the
solutions of all of these are alkaline, which means an indicator can tell you
when you have a neutral solution. The method for finding out exactly how much
of two solutions you need for them to neutralise each other is the
[[titration]] you learned in Chapter 16 (u2:c16): carry out the titration with
an indicator to find the reacting volumes, then mix those same volumes again
without the indicator. This objective is chemistry-only — the whole method is
assessed in Paper 2C only.

**The practical, step by step.**

1. Transfer 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution to a conical flask using a
   pipette, and add a few drops of [[methyl-orange]] as the indicator.
2. Run dilute sulfuric acid in from the burette until the indicator just turns
   from yellow to orange.
3. Note the volume of acid needed, then mix the same volumes of acid and alkali
   together in a clean flask **without any indicator**. The equation for the
   formation of the solution is:

   2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)

4. Heat the solution to evaporate off some of the water until a saturated
   solution is formed, then leave it to cool so that crystals form.
5. Separate the crystals from any remaining solution by filtration (or pour
   the remaining solution away).
6. Dry the crystals by leaving them in a warm place.

The crystallisation process has its own equation:

Na₂SO₄(aq) + 10H₂O(l) → Na₂SO₄·10H₂O(s)

Ten waters of crystallisation for sodium sulfate. To make sodium chloride
crystals instead, you would run dilute hydrochloric acid from the burette
rather than dilute sulfuric acid, then follow the same procedure:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

Ammonium salts come off the same production line. Using
[[ammonium-salt]]s rather than metal salts makes no difference to the method
itself — ammonia solution plays the role the sodium hydroxide solution played:

2NH₃(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → (NH₄)₂SO₄(aq)

Why repeat the titration without the indicator? Because an indicator is an
impurity by design — dye molecules have no business inside a "pure, dry
sample". The first, indicator-carrying titration is a measurement; the second,
indicator-free mixing is the actual preparation.

:::key-point
Why methyl orange can never mark the exact neutral point: below pH 3.1 it is
red and above pH 4.4 it is yellow, so between those pH values it shows a
mixture of the two — orange. That means it is actually yellow at pH 7, so the
colour change does not sit exactly at neutrality. It does not matter: the pH
changes very rapidly near the [[endpoint]] of a titration, so a carefully done
titration still finds the neutralisation point to the nearest drop — which is
excellent.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt,
starting from an acid and alkali" (2.40C, Paper 2C only) scores in beats:
pipette a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask; add a few drops of
indicator; titrate with acid from the burette to the endpoint; record the
volume; repeat the same volumes with **no indicator**; evaporate some water to
saturation; cool to crystallise; filter; dry in a warm place. Two mark-magnets
inside the method: say *why* the titration is repeated without indicator (the
indicator would contaminate the product), and write the equation for the salt
actually named in the question.
:::

:::misconception
"Sodium chloride crystals contain water of crystallisation, like sodium
sulfate does — so the method must be identical in every detail." Simple sodium,
potassium and ammonium salts such as NaCl and (NH₄)₂SO₄ have **no** water of
crystallisation, so in principle you could evaporate all the water in one go
and save time. The disadvantage is the product: powdery crystals or a solid
crust instead of proper crystals. It is always better to concentrate the
solution and let crystals form slowly. And for ammonium salts there is a
second reason: heating dry ammonium salts tends to break them up.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.40C titration-method items. List the six method
beats in order, then answer: why must the titration be repeated without the
indicator, why does the excess-solid method fail here, and why is methyl
orange's colour change not exactly at pH 7 — yet still good enough?
:::

sections.title: Precipitation Reactions
sections.markdown:
Mix silver nitrate solution with sodium chloride solution and the mixture
suddenly clouds: a white solid appears as if from nowhere, hanging in the
liquid. That solid is silver chloride — an [[insoluble]] salt forming from two
soluble ones — and the process that made it is a [[precipitation-reaction]].
This objective is chemistry-only: preparing insoluble salts this way is
assessed in Paper 2C only.

A [[precipitate]] is a solid that is formed by a chemical reaction involving
liquids or gases. A precipitation reaction is simply a reaction that produces a
precipitate. In this reaction, a fine white precipitate of silver chloride is
produced — white precisely because silver chloride will not dissolve in water,
so the solid appears as countless tiny particles suspended in the mixture
before settling. The same reaction appears again in the next chapter wearing a
different hat: mixing a solution containing chloride ions with acidified silver
nitrate solution is *the test* for chloride ions, and the white precipitate is
the positive result.

The chemistry-only flag matters for route planning: Paper 1 never asks you to
describe an insoluble-salt preparation, so if you are sitting Paper 1 only,
this section and the next two are context, not examinable technique. If you are
sitting Paper 2, this is marks on the table — the description questions are
formulaic once you know the pattern.

:::key-point
Chemists' drawings of ions in solution leave the water molecules out to avoid
cluttering the diagram. The water is still there — that is what the (aq) state
symbol means — it is just not drawn. When you sketch ions mixing in a
precipitation reaction, the same convention applies: draw the four ions of
interest, leave the water molecules implied.
:::

:::exam-hint
Name the solid *and* its colour: "a white precipitate of silver chloride"
scores; "a white solid forms" does not. The precipitate's identity comes from
the solubility rules — chlorides except silver and lead(II), so silver
chloride must be the insoluble one. Watch for the gas-trap confusion: nothing
fizzes in this reaction, nothing pops, nothing turns limewater milky — the
only event is a solid appearing in solution.
:::

:::misconception
"The solid must have been sitting in one of the two solutions all along, just
invisible." Nothing was hiding: silver nitrate solution is perfectly clear, and
so is sodium chloride solution. The solid exists only *after* the two
solutions meet — silver ions and chloride ions were both dissolved, free and
separated, until the mixing put them face to face and the attractions became
strong enough to build a lattice. Precipitates are products, not stowaways.
:::

sentence, name the precipitate and its colour when silver nitrate solution
meets sodium chloride solution, and state which paper examines insoluble-salt
preparations.
:::

sections.title: Making Insoluble Salts
sections.markdown:
The basic procedure for making an [[insoluble]] salt is to mix solutions of
two soluble salts. The insoluble salt forms as a [[precipitate]], and a
solution of a soluble one is left behind. For instance, to make insoluble
silver chloride you mix solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride — the
reaction met two sections ago, now with its mechanism opened up.

Silver nitrate solution contains silver ions and nitrate ions in solution. The
positive and negative ions attract each other, but the attractions are not
strong enough to make them stick together. Sodium chloride solution is the
same story: sodium ions and chloride ions, attracted but not stuck. When you
mix the two solutions, the various ions meet each other — and when silver ions
meet chloride ions, the attractions are strong enough that the ions clump
together into a solid. The sodium and nitrate ions remain in solution because
they are not sufficiently attracted to each other. Which ions clump and which
stay free is decided by the solubility rules you already know: silver chloride
is an insoluble exception, sodium nitrate rides the all-soluble first line.

The [[ionic-equation]]s for precipitation reactions are the easiest in the
course to write, because all that happens is that the ions of the insoluble
salt come together to form the solid — the ionic equation simply shows exactly
that. The method has three moves:

- write the formula for the precipitate (the insoluble salt) on the
  right-hand side of the equation
- write the formulae for the ions that come together to produce it on the
  left-hand side
- do not forget the state symbols

For the formation of silver chloride:

Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)

For the formation of barium sulfate:

Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

For the formation of lead(II) iodide — the bright yellow precipitate:

Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s)

You do not need to worry about the spectator ions in these equations, because
they are not doing anything — the sodium, nitrate and leftover ions stay
exactly where they were, dissolved.

:::safety
Wear eye protection. Lead nitrate and lead sulfate are toxic, and all skin
contact must be avoided. Lead(II) iodide shares the hazard — treat every lead
compound in this section as one to measure with a spatula, never with fingers,
and wash hands after the practical even if nothing touched them.
:::

:::exam-hint
The ionic-equation marks are near-automatic if you follow the three moves and
keep the state symbols: aqueous ions on the left, solid precipitate on the
right. Balance charges as you go — lead(II) needs two iodide ions, so
Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s). A favourite extension asks for the ionic
equation of a precipitation you have never seen: the recipe is always "formula
of the insoluble salt on the right; its ions, in solution, on the left."
:::

:::misconception
"The full equation and the ionic equation are two versions of different
reactions." They are the same reaction at two zoom levels. The full equation
records everything present — Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2NaI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq) —
while the ionic equation records everything *happening*: only the two ions
that build the precipitate. The sodium and nitrate ions appear in the full
equation as spectators, unchanged; leaving them out is not simplification for
beginners, it is the honest description of the chemistry.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.41C/2.43C insoluble-salt items. Write full and ionic
equations for the precipitation of barium sulfate from barium chloride solution
and dilute sulfuric acid, with state symbols throughout. Then explain why the
sodium and nitrate ions never appear in the ionic equation.
:::

sections.title: What Do We Mix Together to Make Insoluble Salts?
sections.markdown:
The procedure for making insoluble salts is to mix two solutions of soluble
salts — but how do you know *which* two? Two really useful facts from the
solubility rules decide it:

- all nitrates are [[soluble]]
- all sodium and potassium salts are soluble

So all you have to do is mix the **nitrate** of the metal part of your
[[insoluble]] salt with the **sodium or potassium salt** of the non-metal part.
Both chosen solutions are guaranteed soluble — the nitrate by rule one, the
sodium or potassium salt by the all-soluble first line — and the two unwanted
spectator ions are therefore guaranteed to stay dissolved.

Take lead(II) iodide, the yellow [[precipitate]]. The metal part is lead, so
use a solution of lead(II) nitrate; the non-metal part is iodide, so use a
solution of sodium iodide. The equation for the reaction is:

Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2NaI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq)

Barium sulfate works the same way: use barium nitrate solution and potassium
sulfate solution.

Ba(NO₃)₂(aq) + K₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2KNO₃(aq)

The barium sulfate is a white precipitate. There are other valid pairings too:
barium chloride is soluble, so it works in place of barium nitrate — and the
sulfate part does not have to come from a salt at all, because dilute sulfuric
acid contains sulfate ions, so it can supply them directly.

**The specification's own practical (2.43C): pure, dry lead(II) sulfate.**

1. Take 25 cm³ of lead(II) nitrate solution in a beaker and add 25 cm³ of
   sodium sulfate solution. The amounts do not really matter, because any
   excess will be got rid of later.
2. A white precipitate of lead(II) sulfate forms. The equation is:

   Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq)

3. Filter the reaction mixture. A white residue of lead(II) sulfate is left on
   the filter paper; a colourless solution of sodium nitrate — plus any excess
   reactants — passes through. The white residue is the compound wanted, but
   it is contaminated with the solution clinging to it.
4. Wash the residue with distilled water: pour a 20 cm³ portion (the amount is
   not important) onto the filter paper and let it run through, carrying the
   sodium nitrate and excess reactants with it. Repeat several times so the
   sample is not contaminated with anything.
5. Transfer the filter paper and the lead(II) sulfate to a warm oven to dry —
   the water evaporates and the pure, dry solid remains.

The washing step has a reason worth stating: tap water contains dissolved
substances, so washing with tap water and then drying would leave those
dissolved solids behind on the crystals as they evaporate — contaminating the
very sample the preparation exists to make. Distilled (pure) water leaves
nothing behind.

:::exam-hint
"Choose solutions to make [insoluble salt] X" is a template question: metal
part → its nitrate; non-metal part → the sodium or potassium salt; write the
full equation with the precipitate's state symbol. Marks then move to the
purification beats — filter, wash with *distilled* water, repeat the washing,
dry in a warm oven — and the justify-mark belongs to the word distilled: tap
water would leave its dissolved solids behind on the product. This is also the
lead(II) sulfate practical (2.43C), so it can be asked as a describe-the-
practical with all six beats required.
:::

:::misconception
"Any soluble salt of the metal will do for step one — lead(II) chloride, say."
Lead(II) chloride is *insoluble* — it is on the exception list — so it cannot
be one of your two starting solutions, and it is not "a solution" to begin
with. The nitrate route is not a stylistic preference: the metal's nitrate is
the one soluble salt you can name for *every* metal, which is why the
convention is nitrates for the metal part, sodium or potassium salts for the
non-metal part.
:::

solutions you would mix to make calcium carbonate, and write the full equation.
Then list the four purification beats after precipitation, and justify the

sections.title: Theories of Acids and Bases
sections.markdown:
Chapter 16 (u2:c16) defined acids and alkalis by their ions: an acid is
something that produces H⁺(aq) ions in solution, an alkali something that
produces OH⁻(aq) ions. This ion-in-water definition is called the Arrhenius
theory of acids and bases — and it works perfectly for aqueous chemistry. When
hydrogen chloride gas dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid, the
molecules dissociate to form hydrogen ions:

HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

A neutralisation reaction is then H⁺ from an acid reacting with OH⁻ from an
alkali to form water: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). The problem with the Arrhenius
definition is its boundary: it only applies to reactions that occur in aqueous
solution, and chemistry does not stop at the water's edge. A more general
theory covers more situations:

- **An acid is a proton (hydrogen ion) donor.**
- **A base is a proton (hydrogen ion) acceptor.**

This is the [[bronsted-lowry-theory]], and understanding acids and bases in terms
of [[proton-transfer]] is what this chapter's objectives ask of you. (The
examination does not require you to remember the names of the theories — but
you do need the donor/acceptor definitions cold.) The vocabulary is honest:
a hydrogen atom is one proton with one electron, so if an electron is removed,
only a proton is left — H⁺ *is* a proton.

Rewritten in proton-transfer terms, the reaction when hydrogen chloride
dissolves in water becomes more truthful:

H₂O(l) + HCl(aq) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

The HCl donates (gives) a proton to an H₂O molecule — so the HCl is the acid
and the H₂O is the base, because it accepts the proton. The H₃O⁺(aq) ion is
called the [[hydroxonium-ion]] — this is the ion we usually write simply as
H⁺(aq). You can think of it as a hydrogen ion joined to a water molecule. The
Cl⁻ has its negative charge because the proton left its electron behind when
it transferred to the water.

The ammonium ion you already know is the same idea in another costume: NH₄⁺
is what you get when H⁺ is added to ammonia, NH₃ — and the hydroxonium ion is
the equivalent ion for water. In aqueous solution, ammonia reacts with water
to form OH⁻ ions (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻), which is how ammonia fits the
ion-in-water picture; in proton-transfer terms, the ammonia is simply accepting
a proton from the water. Ammonia and hydrogen chloride do not even need the
water: the two gases react directly to form the white smoke of solid ammonium
chloride — NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s) — a proton handed from HCl to NH₃ with
no solution in sight.

There is even a dot-and-cross story inside the hydroxonium ion. The covalent
bond that forms between the H₂O and the H⁺ is unusual: both of the shared
electrons come from the oxygen. This is called a [[dative-covalent-bond]], or
a co-ordinate covalent bond — and once it has been formed, it is exactly the
same as a "normal" covalent bond.

:::exam-hint
The examination asks you to identify the proton donor and the proton acceptor
in a given reaction — never to name the theories. Read the equation, find who
gives the H⁺ (that is the acid) and who takes it (that is the base). Water
plays both roles across this chapter: accepting a proton from HCl, donating
one to ammonia and to oxide ions. The safest exam sentence is structural:
"the acid donates a proton and the base accepts it."
:::

:::misconception
"An acid must contain H⁺ ions ready-made, so ammonia can never be a base
because it has no hydrogen ion to give." The proton does not have to pre-exist
in the base — the base only has to *accept* one. Ammonia's lone pair reaches
out and takes H⁺ from water (making NH₄⁺) or from HCl (making NH₄Cl); it is
one of the cleanest proton acceptors in the course. Acids donate, bases accept
— contents of the formula are irrelevant to the definition.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.35/2.36 proton-transfer items. Define an acid and a
base in proton-transfer terms, then apply the definitions twice: to
H₂O + HCl → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ (who donates, who accepts?) and to NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl.
Name the ion H₃O⁺ and state what it is usually written as.
:::

sections.title: The Reaction between Ammonia and Hydrogen Chloride
sections.markdown:
Dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with ammonia solution in a neutralisation
reaction to form a salt — ammonium chloride:

NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq)

Ammonium chloride is an ionic salt, so the ions present can be shown
explicitly:

NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

Now the [[proton-transfer]] reading falls out of the equation. In order to form
ammonium chloride, the HCl must donate a proton (H⁺) to the NH₃. The HCl is an
acid because it donates a proton; the NH₃ is a [[base]] because it accepts one.
Ammonia — a molecule with no hydroxide anywhere in it — neutralises an acid
exactly as a hydroxide solution would, and the product is an
[[ammonium-salt]]: the chloride of the ammonium ion.

This one reaction ties three threads of the chapter together. Metal hydroxides
neutralise acids because their OH⁻ accepts H⁺; ammonia neutralises acids
because the nitrogen's lone pair accepts H⁺ directly; and both routes land on
the same ionic product, an ammonium or water molecule plus the acid's anion.
Ammonia's basicity is therefore not a special case bolted onto the rules — it
is the proton-transfer definition doing its job on a molecule the Arrhenius
picture cannot classify on its own.

:::exam-hint
Two sentences win these marks. Product identification: "ammonium chloride, an
ammonium salt" — with the formula NH₄Cl, four hydrogens, not NH₃Cl. Definition
application: "HCl is the acid because it donates a proton; NH₃ is the base
because it accepts one." Examiners also accept the ionic form
NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) as the products — quoting both the formula-unit equation
and the ionic version shows you know the salt is ionic.
:::

:::misconception
"Ammonium chloride must contain ammonium hydroxide, because that's what an
acid plus an alkali gives." The products of this neutralisation are the
ammonium ion and the chloride ion — there is no NH₄OH species hiding in the
equation. Ammonia solution does contain some hydroxide ions (from NH₃ + H₂O ⇌
NH₄⁺ + OH⁻), but the cleanest description writes the direct proton transfer:
NH₃ accepts H⁺ from HCl, and the anion tags along as the counter-ion.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.35/2.36/2.38 ammonia items. Write the equation for
ammonia solution with hydrochloric acid in both formula-unit and ionic form.
Which species donates the proton and which accepts it? And why does this
reaction count as a neutralisation even though ammonia contains no hydroxide
ions?
:::

sections.title: More Acid-base Reactions
sections.markdown:
Acids in solution are acidic because they donate a proton to water, forming
the [[hydroxonium-ion]]. Take a general acid, HA — this is what happens when
it is put into water:

HA(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq)

The HA donates a proton to the H₂O, which acts as a base. For nitric acid this
would be:

HNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)

Bases behave in the mirror-image way. When bases such as metal oxides react
with water, they accept a proton *from* the water — for sodium oxide:

Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2Na⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq)

The O²⁻ ion accepts protons from the water, and in this reaction the water acts
as an acid, because it donates the protons. The same donor/acceptor reading
covers the neutralisations of the earlier sections: when sulfuric acid reacts
with copper(II) oxide,

CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)

the H₂SO₄ is the acid — it donates protons to the CuO, the base. And ammonia
is also a base: it accepts a proton from water,

NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) → NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

What about the classic acid–alkali equation, HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) +
H₂O(l)? [[proton-transfer]] chemistry says what *actually* happens: the H₃O⁺
ion formed when the acid reacts with water donates a proton to the base, OH⁻.
But for International GCSE purposes you almost always use the simplified
version:

H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)

Both sentences describe the same [[neutralisation]] — the simplified equation is
the hydroxonium story with H₃O⁺ abbreviated to H⁺, exactly as the theory
section established. Water's double role is the theme of the whole section: it
accepts a proton from every acid (acting as a base), and donates one to oxide
ions (acting as an acid). It never stops being neutral — these labels describe
what water does *in each reaction*, not what it is in the bottle.

:::exam-hint
Given any equation, the question "state which substance is the acid and which
is the base" is answered by following the H⁺: whoever loses it is the acid,
whoever gains it is the base. Expect water to be cast in either role —
HNO₃ + H₂O makes water the base; Na₂O + H₂O makes water the acid. The
simplified ionic equation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O is what you write for acid–alkali
neutralisation marks; the hydroxonium version is the understanding behind it,
and saying so earns the explain mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Water must be the base in every equation it appears in, because acids are
aqueous." Water's role is decided equation by equation. With an acid (HA +
H₂O → H₃O⁺ + A⁻), water accepts the proton — base. With an oxide ion
(Na₂O + H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻), water donates the proton — acid. The substance
that *donates* in one reaction can *accept* in the next; only the direction of
proton flow in the specific equation decides the labels.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.35/2.36 donor–acceptor items. Write the general
equation for an acid HA in water and state which species is the acid. Then do
the same for sodium oxide with water — and answer the twist question: how can
water be the acid in one equation and the base in another?
:::

sections.title: Choosing the Method of Salt Preparation
sections.markdown:
Every salt preparation in the course is one of three methods, and the choice is
never a matter of taste — two solubility questions decide it. Ask them in
order:

**Question 1: is the salt you want [[soluble]]?** If it is **[[insoluble]]**
(silver chloride, barium sulfate, lead(II) sulfate, most carbonates and
hydroxides), the method is a **[[precipitation-reaction]]**: mix two soluble
solutions — the
metal part as its nitrate, the non-metal part as its sodium or potassium salt —
then filter, wash with distilled water and dry. No acid is needed and no
crystallisation follows, because the product comes out of the reaction as a
solid, not from a solution.

**Question 2 (if the salt is [[soluble]]): is there a suitable solid reactant?**
If the salt can be made from a solid whose excess is visible — a metal from
magnesium to iron, a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide or a carbonate — the method
is the **excess-solid route**: warm the acid, add the solid in excess, filter
off the leftover, crystallise the filtrate. Copper(II) sulfate from copper(II)
oxide and magnesium sulfate from magnesium both ride this route.

**If the salt is soluble but every reactant would be a solution** — the sodium,
potassium and ammonium salts, all of whose compounds dissolve — the method is
the **titration route**: titrate with an indicator to find the reacting
volumes, then mix those volumes again without the indicator and crystallise.
Sodium sulfate from sodium hydroxide solution and sulfuric acid is the
template.

Three examples pin the logic down. Magnesium sulfate: soluble, and magnesium is
a suitable solid — excess-solid route. Sodium nitrate: soluble, but sodium
hydroxide is a solution, so no solid excess is possible — titration route.
Calcium carbonate: insoluble — precipitation route, calcium ions from a soluble
calcium salt (its nitrate or chloride) and carbonate ions from sodium
carbonate solution. The chapter-question bank at this point in the course
drills exactly this classification, salt by salt, with equations — the page
anchor above takes you there for practice.

:::exam-hint
When a question hands you a named salt and asks for the method, answer with
the branch *and* the reagents in one breath: "insoluble, so mix [metal]
nitrate solution with [sodium/potassium] [non-metal part] solution";
"soluble, from excess [solid] with warm [acid]"; "soluble, by titrating
[alkali] against [acid], then repeating without indicator". The follow-up
marks are always the equation and the purification beats — but the branch
choice is the gate every other mark sits behind.
:::

:::misconception
"Acid + metal, acid + base and acid + carbonate are three *methods* of salt
preparation." They are three *reactions* — all inside one single method. The
three methods are the branches above, sorted by solubility: excess-solid,
titration, precipitation. A question asking you to choose a method wants the
branch; a question asking for an equation wants the reaction inside it.
Answering "acid + carbonate" to a method question is like answering "a
spatula" to a question about the plan.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.39/2.40C/2.41C/2.43C method-choice items. Sort
these by method, naming reagents: zinc sulfate, potassium chloride, silver
chloride, copper(II) sulfate (from the oxide), ammonium sulfate. Five salts,
three methods, two solubility questions — the whole chapter in one exercise.
:::

sections.title: End of Chemistry Only
sections.markdown:
This section closes the chapter — and with it, the stretch of Unit 2 that
carries chemistry-only content. Everything the chapter taught now compresses
into ten abilities, one per objective, and each is a question shape you will
meet on the page.

:::summary
A salt is an acid with its hydrogen replaced — by a metal, or by the ammonium
ion — and each acid names its own family: chlorides, nitrates, sulfates,
ethanoates, phosphates. Dilute acids react with metals above hydrogen (metal +
acid → salt + hydrogen, MASH), with bases (metal oxide + acid → salt + water),
and with carbonates in the cold (carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide +
water); the ionic equation Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂ shows why every simple acid
reacts identically. The solubility rules — sodium/potassium/ammonium and
nitrates always soluble; silver and lead(II) chlorides; barium, calcium and
lead(II) sulfates; carbonates and hydroxides insoluble except Na/K/NH₄ — choose
the method: excess solid gives crystals (copper(II) sulfate from copper(II)
oxide, hydrated as CuSO₄·5H₂O); a [[titration]] gives the sodium, potassium and
ammonium salts, repeated without indicator; a [[precipitation-reaction]] gives
the insoluble salts, filtered, washed with distilled water and dried. Beneath it all, acids
are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors: HCl gives H⁺ to water (the
[[hydroxonium-ion]] in disguise), ammonia accepts H⁺ straight from the acid,
and water itself plays both roles.
:::

:::can-you
Keyed to the ten objectives, in order: state the solubility rules and their
exceptions, classifying any named compound (2.34); explain acid–base reactions
as proton transfer (2.35); identify the proton donor and acceptor in a given
equation (2.36); write the equations for hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric
acids with metals, bases and metal carbonates — excluding nitric acid with
metals (2.37); list what can act as a base and define an alkali (2.38);
describe the excess-solid preparation of a pure, dry soluble salt (2.39);
describe the acid + alkali preparation via titration, indicator-free second
run included (2.40C, Paper 2C only); describe the precipitation of an
insoluble salt from two soluble solutions (2.41C, Paper 2C only); walk the
copper(II) sulfate crystal practical end to end (2.42); and describe the
lead(II) sulfate preparation with its distilled-water washing (2.43C, Paper 2C
only).
:::

:::exam-hint
The chemistry-only flag now covers three of the chapter's ten objectives:
2.40C, 2.41C and 2.43C are assessed in Paper 2C only. Paper 1 still examines
the other seven — including both full practical descriptions that are core
(2.39 and 2.42). Plan revision accordingly: if you sit both papers, the three
chemistry-only methods are extra description questions worth methodical
practice; the platform question bank joins every objective by spec ref.
:::

:::misconception
"'Describe an experiment' questions are about the chemistry, so the marks live
in the equation." The marks live in the *sequence*. Every preparation question
in this chapter is scored as an ordered method — reagents, excess or titration
or two-solution mix, filtration, washing, crystallising, drying — and the
equation is one mark among many. Write the method as numbered steps, say *why*
at the two justified moments (excess solid proves the acid is gone; distilled
water protects the dry sample), and the equation lands on top of an answer
that is already most of the way scored.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Salt preparation is an industrial art as much as a lab skill. The ammonium
sulfate route you titrated this chapter is run at tonne scale to make
fertiliser that feeds a measurable share of the world's grain; barium
sulfate's total refusal to dissolve — the solubility rule you learned — is
exactly why it is safe to swallow as a contrast agent for gut X-rays, coating
the tract without entering the blood; and silver chloride's photosensitivity,
first noticed by lab chemists studying precipitates, seeded the entire
photographic industry. The burette technique, the filtration discipline and
the distilled-water standard are the same in a school beaker and a pharmaceutical
plant.
:::
